posts.title: Mingfeng Jiang receives a 2026 National Scholarship
posts.summary: OFEL PhD student Mingfeng Jiang has received a 2026 National Scholarship.
body: Mingfeng Jiang, a PhD student in Fisheries Resources at Shanghai Ocean University and a member of OFEL, has received a 2026 National Scholarship. His research examines how squid populations respond to fishing and environmental change, and how stock assessment models can better reflect their biology.

body.heading: From civil engineering to marine science

body: Mingfeng studied civil engineering as an undergraduate before moving into marine fisheries science for his master’s and doctoral studies. That change of direction led him to research that supports the conservation and sustainable use of marine living resources, with a particular interest in the challenges facing distant-water fisheries.

Working under the supervision of Professor Fan Zhang in the College of Marine Living Resource Sciences and Management, he now focuses on cephalopod population dynamics and assessment methods, especially for jumbo squid (Dosidicus gigas) in the southeast Pacific.

Stock assessments provide the scientific basis for fisheries management, but they must account for the combined effects of fishing, environmental variability and a species’ life history. Cephalopods pose particular challenges: they have short life cycles and respond quickly to changes in ocean conditions, while some species die after spawning. Models developed for longer-lived fish can miss these processes.

In a 2026 first-authored paper in the Journal of Applied Ecology, Mingfeng examined the biases that arise when assessment models ignore death after spawning in semelparous marine species. The study argues that reliable assessments need to represent the biological processes that actually govern a population.

His other work in 2026 explores how the El Niño–Southern Oscillation affects jumbo squid. A paper in Communications Earth & Environment examines how strong El Niño events alter migration routes and reproductive timing in the southeast Pacific. A related study in Ecology and Evolution investigates how growth responses to ENSO differ across locations and life stages.

Mingfeng also studies whether management measures achieve their intended conservation goals. In 2022, he published a first-authored preliminary evaluation of seasonal squid-fishery closures in equatorial high-seas waters of the central and eastern Pacific. A 2024 paper in Fisheries Research used China’s voluntary seasonal closures on the high seas to assess how effectively such measures conserve oceanic squid.

His research extends to tuna fisheries. In Acta Oceanologica Sinica, he examined links between environmental variability and tuna catch composition using the mean trophic level of the catch. He has also developed indicators to inform fishing-access decisions for the western and central Pacific skipjack purse-seine fishery.

At the time of the scholarship profile, he had published five first-authored papers in journals indexed by the Science Citation Index and four in journals indexed by the Chinese Science Citation Database (CSCD).

During 2025 and 2026, Mingfeng gave six oral presentations at international meetings. These included the first and second international symposia on squid conservation and management; a squid workshop of the South Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Organisation’s Scientific Committee; the second Busan dialogue on unregulated fisheries; and an International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas bigeye tuna stock assessment meeting.
He plans to continue studying cephalopod population dynamics and the effects of environmental change, while developing assessment methods that can support fisheries conservation and sustainable use.

This article is adapted from a student profile published on 15 October 2026 by the Graduate Student Union of the College of Marine Living Resource Sciences and Management, Shanghai Ocean University. Original text and photographs: Mingfeng Jiang.

posts.title: Mingfeng Jiang shows that ignoring death after spawning distorts squid stock assessments
posts.summary: A new model, ACLS, treats post-spawning death as part of squid population dynamics, and shows that ignoring it inflates estimates of spawning stock biomass.
body: OFEL PhD student Mingfeng Jiang has developed a stock assessment model for squid and other semelparous species, animals that spawn once and die soon afterwards. The model builds death after spawning directly into the population dynamics, giving a more faithful picture of how these populations change over time. The study is published in the Journal of Applied Ecology.

Semelparous species matter for both ecosystems and fisheries: cephalopods and Pacific salmon together make up about 5% of global marine capture production. Yet most stock assessment models were designed for fish that spawn many times over their lives. When those models are applied to squid, they can misrepresent population dynamics and give a misleading view of stock status.

body.heading: A model built around one spawning

body: The new model, ACLS (an age-structured statistical catch-at-length model for semelparity), removes mature animals from the population once they have spawned, so spent individuals are no longer counted in later time steps. Conventional models carry them forward as if they could spawn again.

body.alt: Technical roadmap: operating models for squid and Pacific salmon feed into two assessment models (ACLS and ACL), followed by misspecification tests and a jumbo squid case study comparing ACLS with ACL, SS3, SPiCT and CMSY.
body.caption: Technical roadmap of the study. Simulated squid and Pacific salmon populations were assessed with ACLS and with a conventional model (ACL), followed by tests of mis-specified inputs and a case study on jumbo squid.
body.credit: Figure 1 from Jiang et al. (2026), Journal of Applied Ecology. © 2026 The Authors.

body.heading: Testing it on squid and salmon

body: Mingfeng and colleagues tested ACLS in simulations covering two contrasting semelparous life histories, short-lived squid and longer-lived Pacific salmon, under different fishing pressures, environmental variability and stock–recruitment relationships. ACLS consistently outperformed the conventional model, estimating population dynamics more accurately and with less bias. Sensitivity tests showed where care is needed: wrong assumptions about natural mortality before spawning, or about the timing of maturity, can reduce its performance.

The simulations also showed what goes wrong when post-spawning death is ignored. The conventional model overestimates biomass in the older age groups, above all the cohort that has already spawned, and this inflates estimates of spawning stock biomass.

Applied to jumbo squid (Dosidicus gigas), ACLS fitted the catch, abundance-index and length-composition data well and showed no evident retrospective bias. Its estimates of key management quantities differed markedly from those of four widely used alternatives: Stock Synthesis 3, the conventional ACL model, SPiCT and Catch-MSY.

The study's message is that population models can only support management credibly if they represent the life history of the species they describe. By accounting for death after spawning, ACLS gives a biologically grounded way to estimate stock status and management reference points for squid and other semelparous species, and a firmer basis for managing cephalopod fisheries sustainably.

Mingfeng Jiang and postdoctoral researcher Sisong Dong are co-first authors. Professor Fan Zhang and Professor Xinjun Chen are co-corresponding authors. The study was carried out with Professor André E. Punt's team at the University of Washington.

paper.title: Ignoring death after spawning misrepresents the population dynamics of marine semelparous species
paper.citation: Jiang, M., Dong, S., Tang, R., Punt, A. E., Zhang, F. & Chen, X. (2026)

posts.title: Xin Cheng maps where and when Pacific tuna vessels drop off AIS tracking
posts.summary: Seven years of AIS records from 1,016 Pacific tuna vessels show that tracking gaps are shrinking, and pinpoint where vessels still go silent.
body: OFEL postdoctoral researcher Xin Cheng has led the first systematic assessment of vessel-tracking data quality for Pacific tuna longline and purse seine fleets. Analysing seven years of Automatic Identification System (AIS) records, the study shows that gaps in the data have fallen steadily, and that the places where vessels drop off the record have stayed the same while shrinking. It is published in npj Ocean Sustainability.

Tuna are among the most valuable fish in the Pacific, and managing them depends on accurate fishing data and estimates of fishing effort. AIS has become a core source for studying vessel behaviour and mapping fishing grounds. Its signals can drop out, though: through equipment faults, signal congestion or patchy coverage, or because a crew switches the transponder off, sometimes to hide illegal fishing. These gaps had never been assessed systematically for Pacific tuna fleets, which limited how far AIS could be trusted in management decisions.

Xin Cheng and colleagues assembled about 130 million high-resolution AIS positions from 1,016 tuna longline and purse seine vessels fishing in the Pacific between 2017 and 2023. They defined an anomaly as a reporting gap, an interval between consecutive signals longer than a set threshold, and tested three thresholds: 60, 90 and 120 minutes. The approach turns data gaps from noise into something that can be counted and mapped.

AIS gaps declined steadily from year to year, with no clear pattern by month or by hour of the day. Coverage now spans almost the entire Pacific fishing area. Gap hotspots stayed in the same places every year but grew smaller, and they are concentrated mainly in waters around Pacific island countries.

Purse seiners lose their signal more often than longliners, and their gaps are more tightly clustered, chiefly near Pacific island countries between about 5°N and 10°S and 140°E and 170°E. Longline hotspots are more scattered, including off northeastern Australia and in open waters of the south-central Pacific.

body.alt: Grid of Pacific Ocean maps for each year from 2017 to 2023, showing AIS gap rates for longline vessels on the left and purse seine vessels on the right at 60, 90 and 120 minute thresholds; dark patches near Pacific island countries fade over the years.
body.caption: Where AIS gaps occur. Gap rates for longline vessels (left, a–c) and purse seine vessels (right, d–f) in each year from 2017 to 2023, using thresholds of 60, 90 and 120 minutes. Darker blue means a higher share of gaps; hotspots persist but fade over time.
body.credit: Figure 5 from Cheng et al. (2026), npj Ocean Sustainability. Licensed under CC BY 4.0.

body: The results confirm that AIS data are usable, and improving, as a foundation for fisheries research, and they show where monitoring effort is most needed. The authors suggest that regional fisheries management organisations work with coastal states to target the persistent hotspots around Pacific island countries, and that AIS gaps be tracked routinely as a basis for differentiated, data-driven oversight of fishing fleets.
Xin Cheng is the first author. Lecturer Qinqin Lin and Professor Xinjun Chen are co-corresponding authors.

paper.title: Spatio-temporal variation of AIS data abnormally for tuna fishing fleets in the Pacific Ocean
paper.citation: Cheng, X., Li, H., Feng, J., Lin, Q. & Chen, X. (2026)

posts.title: Mingfeng Jiang shows how strong El Niño events reshape jumbo squid migration and spawning
posts.summary: Machine learning applied to 28 years of fishery and ocean data shows that strong El Niño events bring jumbo squid spawning forward and shorten their migrations, driven mainly by sea surface temperature.
body: OFEL PhD student Mingfeng Jiang has shown how the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) reshapes the spawning migration of jumbo squid (Dosidicus gigas) in the southeast Pacific. Using ensemble machine learning on data from 1997 to 2024, the study is the first systematic analysis of how the species' migration and reproductive timing respond to ENSO events, and it identifies sea surface temperature as the main driver of the changes. The paper is published in Communications Earth & Environment.

body.heading: A sensitive species in a changing ocean

body: Jumbo squid account for more than a quarter of the world's cephalopod catch. They are the main target of the high-seas squid jigging fishery in the southeast Pacific and a key link in the ocean food web. As short-lived, cold-blooded migrants, they respond strongly to changes in the ocean, yet how their migration and spawning are regulated had not been worked out quantitatively.

Mingfeng and colleagues combined biological measurements from the fishery (mantle length, body weight and gonad development) with ocean data on temperature, dissolved oxygen and chlorophyll at different depths. They first separated the squid into small, medium and large groups, then focused on the large group. A stacking ensemble of five machine-learning models predicted where these squid occur through the year, and an interpretation method (SHAP) showed which environmental factors drove the predictions under each ENSO phase.

body.alt: Technology roadmap: biological data (mantle length, body weight, gonad level and weight) and environmental data (vertical temperature, dissolved oxygen and chlorophyll) feed a subpopulation classification and a stacking ensemble model (random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, SVM and neural network, combined by glmnet), whose predictions are analysed for ENSO-specific migration distances and environmental mechanisms.
body.caption: Technology roadmap of the study, from biological and environmental data through subpopulation classification and a stacking ensemble model to ENSO-specific migration distances and their environmental drivers.
body.credit: Figure 1 from Jiang et al. (2026), Communications Earth & Environment. Licensed under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; reproduced without changes.

body.heading: What changes in an El Niño year

body: Jumbo squid follow a clear annual migration cycle, and ENSO alters it. During strong El Niño periods the spawning peak comes about a month earlier, migration distances shrink to roughly 50–70% of those in La Niña years, and migration routes shift south-eastward toward the coast.

Two environmental factors stood out. Surface dissolved oxygen is the main factor limiting where the squid aggregate, while sea surface temperature drives the change in migration during El Niño. The large group's preference for cooler water provides the physiological basis for its response to ENSO-related temperature swings.

The team suggests that warmer-than-normal surface water in El Niño years, by bringing spawning forward, may lower egg hatching success and cause young squid to mature early, eventually reducing the population's biomass. Because extreme El Niño events are expected to become longer and more frequent as the climate warms, these results help anticipate future changes in a commercially important species and support a shift from static to dynamic management of high-seas cephalopod fisheries.
Mingfeng Jiang is the first author. Professor Xinjun Chen and Professor Fan Zhang are co-corresponding authors.

posts.title: Runze Wang reveals how differently tuna assessments around the world handle model uncertainty
posts.summary: A review of 133 stock assessments from five tuna management organisations shows that choices about model uncertainty follow the organisation more than the species, and proposes best practices to make them more consistent.
body: OFEL master's student Runze Wang has produced the first systematic analysis of how model uncertainty is specified in tuna stock assessments worldwide. The study shows that these choices vary widely, that they depend more on the management organisation than on the biology of the species, and that subjective judgement plays a substantial role. It is published in Fish and Fisheries.

Tuna are among the world's most important marine fishery resources, and their sustainable use depends on sound stock assessments. Model uncertainty is a major source of scientific uncertainty in those assessments. It is usually explored through sensitivity analyses and model ensembles, but which factors are included, and at what levels, differs both within and among the tuna Regional Fisheries Management Organisations (tRFMOs).

Runze and colleagues reviewed the uncertainty specifications in 133 stock assessments carried out over the past 20 years by five tRFMOs, covering seven major commercial tuna species. They compared which uncertainty factors each assessment included, how similar assessments were to one another, and what explained changes between successive assessments of the same stock.

Although a wide range of uncertainty specifications has been used, only a few factors are considered in most assessments. Patterns line up more closely with the management organisation than with the species: assessments within one organisation tend to look alike even for different tunas, suggesting that institutional practice shapes these choices more than biology does.

The emphasis has also shifted over time. Uncertainty related to data, such as data weighting, has received less attention, while biological processes such as growth have received more. Between successive assessments of the same stock, changes in modelling approach, along with changes in fleet structure and stock definitions, were the main reasons the uncertainty specification changed.

The authors recommend cross-organisation coordination and expert review to make assessment methods more consistent and transparent, together with a standardised checklist of uncertainties so that every potential source is considered and individual analysts' preferences carry less weight. They also set out best-practice guidance that walks assessment teams step by step through selecting and specifying uncertainty.

Runze Wang and postdoctoral researcher Sisong Dong are co-first authors, and Professor Fan Zhang is the corresponding author. Co-authors include André E. Punt of the University of Washington and Jiangfeng Zhu of Shanghai Ocean University.

paper.title: Diversity and Subjectivity of Model Uncertainty Specification in Global Tuna Stock Assessment
paper.citation: Wang, R., Dong, S., Punt, A. E., Zhu, J. & Zhang, F. (2026)

posts.title: Fan Zhang appointed Chair of ICCAT's Working Group on Stock Assessment Methods
posts.summary: OFEL's principal investigator is the first scientist from China to chair an ICCAT working group since the country joined the Commission in 1996.
body: The International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT) has appointed Professor Fan Zhang, principal investigator of OFEL, as Chair of its Working Group on Stock Assessment Methods (WGSAM). The group sits under ICCAT's Standing Committee on Research and Statistics (SCRS). Fan Zhang is the first scientist from China to chair an ICCAT working group since China joined the Commission in 1996.

ICCAT is the intergovernmental organisation responsible for the conservation and management of tunas and tuna-like species in the Atlantic Ocean and adjacent seas, with its Secretariat in Madrid. The SCRS is its scientific advisory body, and it and its working groups meet several times each year to discuss stock assessments, management measures and science-based decision-making. WGSAM leads the Commission's work on stock assessment methods, coordinating approaches internationally and advancing new techniques.

body.heading: A role that matches the lab's research

body: Fan Zhang is China's chief scientist for ICCAT and has long worked on stock assessment models and management strategies. The appointment connects closely with OFEL's research on assessment methods, from how uncertainty is specified in tuna assessments to new models for species with unusual life histories, and with the lab's wider involvement in regional fisheries management organisations.
